pages.heading: A clearer model for React
pages.text:
A component describes the interface for a particular
 set of props, state and context. Rendering calculates
 that description; committing applies the necessary
 changes to the screen.


        Inputs                  Render        Commit




 Keep rendering pure: do not change unrelated objects,
 start requests or subscribe to events while calculating
 the interface.

 Reading question: what belongs in rendering, and what
 belongs in an event handler?

pages.heading: State is a snapshot
Keys describe identity
pages.text:
A stable key helps React match an item to its previous
 instance within a list of siblings. Reordering should
 not make one item inherit the local state of another.
 items.map(item => (
   <Row key={item.id} item={item} />
 ));


 An array index can be a poor key when items move,
 are inserted or removed. A freshly generated random
 key also destroys continuity between renders.

 Practice: explain why editing a row can reveal a bad key
 choice.

pages.heading: Start with the job
pages.text:
Before drawing components, establish who uses the
 system, what they need to do, and what failure would
 mean. An architecture solves a particular set of
 constraints.


         Need                   Constraint    Decision




 For a personal PDF reader, local access, data integrity
 and fast navigation may matter more than
 multi-region availability. Do not pay for complexity
 that the task does not require.

 A useful question: what must still work when the
 internet does not?

pages.heading: Make data ownership clear
pages.text:
Give each responsibility an owner. The interface
 presents state. An application service coordinates a
 workflow. Persistence commits durable changes.


         View                   Use case       Storage




 Passing a database object through every screen makes
 boundaries difficult to change. Passing an immutable
 document summary keeps rendering separate from
 storage details.

 Identify which layer should know about file paths, and
 which should only know about a document identifier.

pages.heading: Caching is a tradeoff
pages.text:
A cache avoids repeating work, but introduces a
 second representation that can become stale. Decide
 what is authoritative, how entries are invalidated and
 how much memory the cache may use.

 PDF thumbnails are derived data. If a thumbnail
 disappears, recreate it. Original documents and
 private annotations are not disposable caches.


       Original                 Thumbnail     Display




 Ask: can this information be recreated without asking
 the user to do the work again?

pages.heading: Design the failure path
pages.text:
An import is not complete when a preview appears. It
 is complete when the required data has been safely
 stored and the operation has been acknowledged.

 A recoverable design considers full storage,
 interrupted writes, duplicate requests and corrupted
 input. Error messages must tell the user what
 happened without claiming that missing work was
 saved.
 This is original sample material illustrating general engineering reasoning.
 The architecture and recovery semantics of this app are documented in the
 source package.

 Review exercise: sketch a save operation that can fail at
 any step without overwriting the original.

pages.heading: Know the return shape
pages.text:
Choosing an array method starts with the shape you
 need back. One item, a new array and a yes-or-no
 answer are different results.
 items.find(test);      // item or undefined
 items.filter(test); // array
 items.some(test);      // boolean
 items.every(test);     // boolean


 Find selects the first matching value. Filter creates an
 array containing matching values. Some asks whether
 a match exists; every asks whether all visited items
 pass.

 A boolean cannot be followed by .map(). Check the
 return value before chaining methods.

pages.heading: Return is not decoration
A closure keeps access
Change a value, keep the original
pages.text:
To update an item without mutating the source array,
 create a new array and a new object for the item that
 changes.
 const updated = games.map(game =>
   game.title === "Eclipse"
      ? { ...game, favorite: true }
      : game
 );


 Unchanged objects are reused here. This is a shallow
 update, not a deep clone of every nested object.
 Primary reading: developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Referen
 ce/Global_Objects/Array
 developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Closures

pages.heading: Make the boundary visible
pages.text:
A pattern is useful when it makes a recurring design
 problem easier to understand. It is not a requirement
 to put every application behind layers of indirection.


       Contract                 Adapter       System




 For a PDF reader, a small interface for storing library
 metadata lets the application service work with a disk
 implementation or a test double.

 A new engineer should know what a module owns
 before reading its implementation.

pages.heading: One reason to change
pages.text:
Keep rendering, workflow decisions and durable
 storage separate. A typography change should not
 require editing a file-import transaction.

 Small files help, but file length alone does not
 guarantee good boundaries. A module should expose
 a coherent contract and avoid leaking details that
 callers do not need.

 Try naming a module without using the words manager,
 helper or utils.

pages.heading: Depend on a contract
pages.text:
An application workflow can depend on a storage
 contract instead of constructing a specific database or
 file store. The composition root supplies the concrete
 implementation.
 protocol LibraryPersistence {
     func load() throws -> Library
     func save(_ library: Library) throws
 }


 This keeps tests focused. A storage failure can be
 introduced deliberately without filling the device or
 corrupting real user files.

 Test that an unsuccessful save does not leak
 uncommitted in-memory state.

pages.heading: Use patterns sparingly
pages.text:
Every abstraction introduces a concept that the next
 engineer must learn. Add the boundary when it
 protects a responsibility, enables an important test or
 isolates a volatile dependency.

 Keep the simplest implementation that meets the real
 constraints. An offline personal library does not need
 a distributed backend to look or feel well made.
 This sample explains the design approach used in Shelf. The architecture
 and decision records in the source package describe the actual
 implementation.

 What can you remove without weakening a guarantee
 the user depends on?

pages.heading: A model is a simplification
pages.text:
A useful model keeps the details that affect a decision
 and leaves out those that do not. It should help you
 reason, not merely give something a more impressive
 name.

 For example, describing a stack as last-in, first-out
 helps predict which item is removed next. The
 description is useful before deciding how to store the
 stack.


        Push A                  Push B         Pop B




 Use a tiny concrete example before introducing an
 abstraction.

pages.heading: Growth, not a stopwatch
pages.text:
Time complexity describes how work grows with
 input size under a stated model. It does not predict the
 exact time on a particular device.

 A linear scan may inspect every element. A binary
 search repeatedly narrows a sorted search space. The
 latter relies on a precondition: the data must have a
 compatible ordering.

 Ask whether preparation and sorting costs are included
 in the analysis.

pages.heading: References and copies
pages.text:
Two variables can refer to the same mutable object.
 Changing that object through one variable is visible
 through the other reference.
 const a = { score: 1 };
 const b = a;
 b.score = 2;
 console.log(a.score); // 2


 Copying an outer object with spread does not
 automatically copy its nested objects. The boundary
 between shared and copied data matters.

 Draw two arrows pointing to the same object. The bug
 becomes easier to see.

pages.heading: Use the right structure
pages.text:
The important question is not which data structure is
 most sophisticated. It is which operations must be
 cheap, which ordering matters and what guarantees
 the caller needs.

 A library may keep its original files by stable
 identifier while maintaining a separate searchable
 metadata representation. Different representations
 serve different operations.
 Original sample material. JavaScript reference semantics: developer.mozilla.
 org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Working_with_objects

 Before optimizing, list the three operations your
 application performs most often.

pages.heading: Reason before typing
pages.text:
State the expected input and output. Ask about empty
 input, duplicates, ordering and invalid values before
 choosing an algorithm.


        Clarify                 Example        Implement




 A small example is useful because it makes hidden
 assumptions visible. It is easier to correct the contract
 before coding than to retrofit it into a finished
 implementation.

 What does a successful result look like for an empty
 input?

pages.heading: Trace the program
pages.text:
Read a short program in execution order. Track the
 value produced by each expression and the value
 returned by each function.
 const numbers = [1, 2, 3];
 const kept = numbers.filter(n => n > 1);
 const doubled = kept.map(n => n * 2);
 console.log(doubled); // [4, 6]


 A useful trace records both type and value. A result
 can look semantically related to the task while having
 the wrong shape for the next operation.

 Try the same reasoning with no matching numbers.
 Does your chain still work?

pages.heading: Test the boundary
pages.text:
Test cases should probe the assumptions, not merely
 confirm the example used while writing the code.
 Include the smallest input, a repeated value and a case
 that challenges ordering.
 function firstEven(values) {
     return values.find(value => value % 2 === 0);
 }
 firstEven([]);          // undefined
 firstEven([3, 5]);      // undefined
 firstEven([3, 4, 2]); // 4


 Explain what the caller should do when a result is
 undefined.

pages.heading: Explain the tradeoff
pages.text:
A technically correct solution is only part of the
 conversation. Explain the assumptions, the chosen
 approach and the cost as the input grows.

 Avoid claiming that one implementation is faster
 without defining the input, runtime and measurement.
 Simpler code can be the better default until a
 demonstrated bottleneck requires more work.
 These are original sample practice notes. No scoring, generated questions or
 interview simulation is running inside Shelf.

 Write one note: what would make you change your
 chosen solution?
